blocks.text: The frictional effect between different layers of a flowing fluid is described in terms of the viscosity of the fluid. Viscosity measures how much force is required to slide one layer of the liquid over another layer. Substances that do not flow easily, such as thick tar and honey, have large coefficients of viscosity, usually denoted by the Greek letter eta; substances which flow easily, like water, have small coefficients of viscosity. Since liquids and gases have non-zero viscosity, a force is required if an object is to be moved through them. Even the small viscosity of the air causes a large retarding force on a car travelling at high speed; if you stick your hand out of the window of a fast-moving car you can easily recognise that considerable force has to be exerted on your hand to move it through the air.

blocks.title: Drag force
blocks.text: An object moving through a fluid experiences a retarding force called a drag force. The drag force increases as the speed of the object increases.

Even in the simplest cases the exact value of the drag force is difficult to calculate; the case of a sphere moving through a fluid, however, is of great importance. The drag force F on a sphere of radius r moving slowly with speed v through a fluid of viscosity eta is given by Stokes' law: F = 6 pi eta r v ... (5.28). At high speeds, however, the force is no longer simply proportional to the speed.

blocks.text: A chimney works best when it is tall and exposed to air currents, which reduce the pressure at the top and force the upward flow of smoke (Do You Know).

blocks.alt: A brick chimney rises from a fireplace with a fire through a roof slab. White smoke with upward blue arrows rises up the flue. Blue lines of wind blow across the top of the chimney, and the smoke leaving the top bends away with them.
